page: Microsoft Azure L48as_v4 is a storage-oriented virtual machine belonging to the Lasv4 server family. It is powered by an AMD EPYC 9V74 processor utilizing the x86_64 architecture, featuring 48 vCPUs across 24 physical cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU operates at a clock speed of 3.7 GHz and includes dedicated allocation. The hardware configuration is equipped with 384.0 GB of system memory, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. For local storage, the instance includes 11,519 GB of capacity and is Premium Storage capable, operating under the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor.

In benchmark evaluations, the L48as_v4 demonstrates strong CPU and memory performance, placing in the top 25% for both stress-ng single-core and multi-core tests. This processing capability is supported by AVX-512 vector extensions, including AVX512_VNNI and AVX512_BF16, which contribute to top-tier performance in small-model LLM prompt processing at 3,802.16 tokens per second. Memory performance is mixed; while cached small-block read bandwidth is in the top 25%, uncached large-block read and write bandwidths fall into the middle 50% tier.

The instance exhibits clear performance tradeoffs when handling larger computational models. While small-scale LLM inference is highly efficient, text generation using a large 70B model drops to a poor 2.53 tokens per second, placing it in the bottom 10%. Database operations and static web serving throughput also register in the average tier. Given the combination of 11.5 TB of local storage, 384 GB of RAM, and strong multi-threaded decompression capabilities, this server is configured for large-scale database hosting, data warehousing, and memory-intensive storage workloads rather than heavy LLM text generation.

It is equipped with 384.0 GB of RAM and a substantial 11,519 GB of local storage. Benchmarks indicate strong CPU and memory performance, placing in the top 25% for stress-ng and Geekbench tests, alongside top-tier prompt processing speeds for small LLM models. However, uncached memory bandwidth and large-model text generation represent notable performance tradeoffs, with 70B model generation falling into the bottom 10%. This hardware profile is suited for large-scale database deployments, memory-intensive storage applications, and data warehousing workloads that benefit from high local storage capacity and dedicated compute resources.
